Investors often weigh the safety of household staples against the excitement of growth brands. Let's see if Kraft Heinz (NYSE:KHC) or On (NYSE:ONON) is the better buy for your portfolio.

Kraft Heinz operates as a global food giant with iconic household brands, while On is a Swiss athletic brand disrupting the footwear market. While they serve different consumer needs, both companies are vying for space in diversified portfolios, making them an interesting pair to compare for long-term growth and stability.

The case for Kraft Heinz

The company focuses on its North America Retail and International Developed Markets segments, moving brands like Heinz and Philadelphia through a vast distribution network. Walmart (NASDAQ:WMT) is the largest customer, representing nearly 21% of net sales, and customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business. Kraft Heinz also provides products for many foodservice distributors, reaching consumers in restaurants and on the go.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 26, 2026, revenue reached nearly $24.8 billion, representing a decrease of approximately 1.5% compared to the prior year. The company reported a net loss of close to $3.5 billion during this same period. This decline in revenue suggests a challenging environment for top-line growth as consumer spending patterns shift.

The debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 0.5x as of its December 2025 balance sheet. This ratio measures total debt against shareholder equity, where a lower number indicates less reliance on borrowed money. The current ratio, which measures a company's ability to pay short-term obligations with short-term assets, was approximately 1.2x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 27, 2025, free cash flow was close to $3.7 billion.

The case for On

On focuses on a premium performance strategy, selling high-end running shoes and apparel through a mix of wholesale partners and its own retail stores. The brand has expanded rapidly across the Americas and Asia-Pacific, relying on a premium image to attract athletes and lifestyle consumers alike. By controlling its direct-to-consumer channels, the company maintains higher oversight of its brand presentation and customer relationships.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached approximately $4.0 billion, a significant increase of roughly 17.4% year over year. Net income for this period was close to $527.4 million. This strong growth in both revenue and net income highlights the brand's momentum in the global footwear and apparel market.

title: Retailers Sanguine for Black Friday

Retailers Sanguine for Black Friday
David Moin

WMT
TGT
ANF
KSS

Trading disclosure

It's crunch time for retailers — and the challenges this holiday season loom large.

Retailers are up against cost-conscious, cash-strapped consumers demanding greater value, deeper discounts and more conveniences. They're also dealing with rising logistics and fuel costs, shifting tariffs, El Niño disrupting the weather and sudden concerns that the anticipated surge in online retail orders and AI could cause outages, following the Federal Aviation Administration, JPMorgan Chase, Microsoft, and other outages this month.

More from WWD

From Peptides and NAD Supplements to 'Nature's Ozempic,' These Black Friday Deals Save You Up to 50% Off Top Wellness Trends

From Prada Sunglasses to Viral Reformation Silk Pants, Nordstrom's Black Friday Sale Has Plenty to Covet - Including Finds Under $100

How Crucial Is Black Friday Weekend to Retailers?

Yet the positive outlook for decent holiday sales gains remains intact — at least for now — with consumers showing resilience so far and a greater inclination to visit stores, a trend particularly true for Gen Z. They're helping retailers keep it together. Positive third-quarter results from Walmart, Target, Abercrombie & Fitch, Gap brand, and even Kohl's, as well as lower temperatures this week, suggest there's momentum ahead of Black Friday.

Retailers also have 29 days between Thanksgiving and Christmas this year, one more than last year.

Toys are selling at Kohl's following improvements in the presentation.

Coats and cold-weather merchandise have not been selling well, but consumer demand for rainwear and wet-weather categories will increase this holiday weekend, according to Planalytics, which advises retailers on the weather and its impact on business. "Overall, the weather over the entire Black Friday weekend will favor winter-driven categories such as outerwear, boots, hats and gloves, blankets and seasonal food and beverages as shoppers respond to both promotions and the more wintry feel," said Evan Gold, executive vice president of global partnerships and alliances at Planalytics.

"By midweek colder air will slide across the central and eastern U.S. and the West will turn warmer again. Finally the colder air will settle over the Southeast at the end of the week and warmer conditions will prevail over the rest of the U.S. Rain will fall in the East and West Coast for much of the week, including heavy rain and high winds in the Midwest and Northeast on Thanksgiving Day and into Black Friday, including New York City, Boston and Philadelphia. Most of the U.S. will be warmer than last year and warmer than normal with a sliver of colder anomalies along the Gulf Coast. Showers will continue near all three coastlines, while the interior of the country is dry."

title: 3 Unstoppable Stocks That Can Be Great Buys for Decades

3 Unstoppable Stocks That Can Be Great Buys for Decades
David Jagielski, CPA, The Motley Fool
Tue, November 24, 2026 at 2:42 PM EST 5 min read
NVDA
AMZN
MSFT
WMT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Stocks that are great long-term investments have solid underlying financials, and there's a great deal of predictability around their futures. What the recent Nvidia scandal has brought to light is the importance of investing in a business that may not be highly dependent on just a single person or the outlook for artificial intelligence (AI).

Three companies that look like unstoppable investments for the long term, regardless of what happens with AI, are Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), and Walmart (NASDAQ:WMT). Here's why they can make for excellent buy-and-forget investments.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Amazon

Amazon's stock hasn't gotten much love over the past year. While it has generated decent 12% returns over the past 12 months, that pales in comparison to some of the gains tech stocks have accumulated over that stretch.

But for a company that's typically at the forefront of any tech innovation, its modest gains can actually be excellent news for investors who buy the stock today. While its financial results have been improving, its valuation hasn't taken off, and thus, it has become a much more attractive investment in the process.

The stock is currently trading at 23 times its expected future profits (based on analyst projections). That's a modest valuation for one of the leading tech companies in the world. It's developing robotaxis, its own AI chips, and deploying drones for delivery, among other opportunities it's pursuing. On top of all that is, of course, its massive e-commerce business.

To buy such a tremendous stock at a low valuation could prove to be a steal of a deal in the future.

Microsoft

Another tech giant that I like for the long haul is Microsoft. It's been a top name in tech for decades, and the reason I don't see that changing is because of how trusted and entrenched its software is within corporate environments. Businesses rely on Microsoft's Office software on a daily basis.

While there have been other options and there will continue to be more competition in the future, I think the reliability that its software offers and the trust it has built up over the years is what gives it a huge competitive advantage. And the company's investments in AI could also pay off significantly, with Microsoft's Office software now able to do much more, with its Copilot assistant helping create spreadsheets and documents in just minutes, potentially saving corporate clients hours each day.

Credit: Getty Images

Buy-and-hold dividend growth investors know something about the best dividend stocks to buy that less experienced yield-hunters don't: it pays to be patient when you're investing for income.

Shares in companies that raise their payouts like clockwork decade after decade can produce superior total returns (price change plus dividends) over the long run, even if they sport apparently ho-hum yields to begin with.

That's partly because regular dividend increases lift the yield on an investor's original cost basis. Stick around long enough, and the modest yield you received on your initial investment can hit double digits one day.

Companies with long histories of annual dividend growth also offer some peace of mind. After all, any company that manages to raise its dividend year after year — through recession, war, market crashes and more — is demonstrating both its financial resilience and its commitment to returning cash to shareholders.

What can dividend growth stocks do for long-term returns?

"The S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats exhibits both capital growth and dividend income characteristics," writes Rupert Watts, head of factors and dividends at S&P Dow Jones Indices. "Over the long term, the S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats exhibited higher returns with lower volatility compared with the S&P 500, resulting in higher risk-adjusted returns."

Put another way, dividend growers not only go along for the ride in bull markets, but they also tend to hold up better in market drawdowns.

Case in point: The S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats Index lost 6.2% on a total return basis in 2022 — better than the S&P 500's 18.1% decline.

And dividends are an important element of overall returns, say Argus Research Director of Portfolio Strategies John Eade and Director of Research Jim Kelleher.

Citing data from Ned Davis Research, the two note that the average annual return of stocks within the S&P 500 between 1972 and 2010 was 7.3%, but the average annual return for companies that initiated or raised their dividends was 9.6%.

"Stable and increasing dividends also act as a signal of management's confidence in their firm's prospects," Watts adds. Additionally, investors consider such track records as a sign of corporate maturity and balance sheet strength.

How do you find the best dividend stocks to buy?
Credit: Getty Images

If you're looking to add dependable dividend growers to your portfolio, you can start by checking out the S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats, an index of 69 companies in the S&P 500 that have raised their payouts annually for at least 25 consecutive years.

title: Symbotic Q4 Earnings Call Details Walmart Deal and Revenue Timing
detail:
Symbotic Q4 Earnings Call Details Walmart Deal and Revenue Timing
Zacks Equity Research
Tue, November 24, 2026 at 11:13 AM EST 4 min read
SYM
WMT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Symbotic Inc. SYM expects its expanded Walmart agreement to add nearly $7 billion to backlog in the first quarter of fiscal 2027. The deal adds work at existing U.S. distribution centers and extends its international reach.

Chief financial officer Izilda Martins said the agreement will have a greater impact in later years than in fiscal 2027. She told Goldman Sachs the program will extend beyond the end of the decade.

SYM Expects More Revenues in the Second Half

Symbotic expects first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenues of $805 million to $825 million and adjusted EBITDA of $110 million to $120 million. Martins expects fiscal 2027 revenues to be slightly more weighted toward the second half than in fiscal 2026.

Asked by Barclays about the $22.3 billion in quarter-end backlog, Martins reaffirmed that Symbotic expects to deliver 16% of it in fiscal 2027, with about 45% of that amount in the first half and 55% in the second.

When Craig-Hallum asked whether that split implied a sequential revenue decline in the fiscal second quarter, Martins said she expects sequential growth. The backlog disclosure covers systems and software. Operations services contribute additional revenues.

Symbotic Adds Storage for Walmart's Online Business

In response to Citigroup, chairman and chief executive officer Richard Cohen said denser storage will let Walmart carry more inventory for online orders inside its existing U.S. distribution centers.

The deal also covers automation at new buildings in Walmart's international network.

Baird asked when Walmart's $125 million development commitment would start contributing revenues. Martins pointed to the latter part of fiscal 2027. Cohen said the research will include ways to improve how Walmart handles online inventory at its distribution centers.

SYM Sets a Timeline for In-Store Fulfillment

Symbotic is installing two SymMicro systems at Walmart stores to automate the picking of individual items for online orders. Cohen told Goldman Sachs that the first site is expected to go live in January 2027 and the second about six months later.

The installations are a step toward a potential 400-store order worth more than $5 billion in additional backlog. Cohen said lessons from the first two prototypes and software simulations helped accelerate the next design.

Cohen told Oppenheimer that smaller sites required a robot with a different payload and upgraded software. Symbotic has robots working with frozen and perishable goods in its back-of-store systems.
